h1. Goal

Provide documentation and examples for using RBAC and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to grant scoped permissions to specific users for ClusterExtension and ClusterObjectSet writes, now that OLMv1 operates with cluster-admin scope.

h2. Why is this important?

With the shift to cluster-admin scope, the security boundary moves from per-extension ServiceAccounts to access control on the ClusterExtension and ClusterObjectSet APIs themselves. Cluster administrators need clear guidance and examples for how to:

* Control who can create/modify ClusterExtensions
* Restrict which extensions specific users can install (e.g. by source, package name, namespace)
* Use ValidatingAdmissionPolicy for fine-grained policy enforcement

This is the new answer to "how do I grant scoped permissions?" in OLMv1.

h2. Description

When granting non-cluster-admin users restricted permission to write ClusterExtensions, a cluster admin needs to do two things:

* Create VAP that restricts what they can set in a ClusterExtension (if VAP is granted without RBAC, users will still have no permission to managed ClusterExtensions)
* Grant the user/group RBAC permission to manage clusterextensions (if RBAC is granted without VAP, users may be able to escalate permissions)

TL;DR:

* VAP is used to lock ClusterExtension permissions down to be granular
* RBAC is required to open up permissions, but RBAC is too broad by itself.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* Documentation explaining the new permission model (cluster-admin controller, RBAC on CE/COS APIs)
* Examples of RBAC + ValidatingAdmissionPolicy configurations for common delegation scenarios:
** Allow a user to create/manage only specific ClusterExtensions
** Allow a group to manage extensions in specific namespaces
** Restrict which ClusterCatalogs a user/group can reference
** Restrict which packages a user/group can install
** Restrict namespace targets
* Migration guidance for users transitioning from SA-based permission control

h2. Dependencies

* Blocked by: OPRUN-4630 (Deprecate spec.serviceAccount and adopt cluster-admin scope)

items.toString:
h1. Goal

Refactor the Helm content manager and Boxcutter runtime from per-CE/SA scoped caches and clients to a single global/shared cache, now that all operations use the same controller identity.

h2. Why is this important?

With the adoption of cluster-admin scope (OPRUN-4630), all CE and COS reconciliation uses the operator-controller's own SA. The per-CE/SA scoped caches and per-COS scoped clients were designed for a world where each extension had its own identity — that's no longer the case. A single global cache is simpler, more efficient, and eliminates the overhead of creating and managing per-extension dynamic clients and informer factories.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* CI - MUST be running successfully with tests automated
* Helm content manager ({{internal/operator-controller/contentmanager/}}) refactored from per-CE caches to a single global cache

* {{RestConfigMapper}} pattern removed or simplified (no longer maps per-CE)

* Single {{DynamicSharedInformerFactory}} shared across all CEs

* {{Manager.Get()}} no longer creates per-CE dynamic clients

* Boxcutter runtime refactored to use a shared client instead of per-COS scoped clients (if applicable)

* {{revision_engine_factory.go:createScopedClient}} removed or simplified

* Per-COS {{TokenInjectingRoundTripper}} usage eliminated

* No behavioral regression in drift detection or managed content watching
* All unit and e2e tests updated

h2. Key code areas

* {{internal/operator-controller/contentmanager/contentmanager.go}} — refactor {{Manager}} from per-CE to global cache
* {{internal/operator-controller/contentmanager/sourcerer.go}} — simplify dynamic sourcerer
* {{internal/operator-controller/contentmanager/cache/}} — simplify cache interface if needed
* {{internal/operator-controller/controllers/revision_engine_factory.go}} — remove {{createScopedClient}}, use shared client
* {{cmd/operator-controller/main.go}} — simplify content manager initialization

items.toString:
h1. Goal

Remove the {{PreflightPermissions}} alpha feature gate and all associated pre-authorization code, including the {{authorization/}} package and the {{k8s.io/kubernetes}} dependency.

h2. Why is this important?

With OLMv1 adopting cluster-admin scope, pre-authorization checks that validate whether a ServiceAccount has the right permissions before applying manifests are unnecessary — the controller always has permission. Removing this code also eliminates the heavyweight {{k8s.io/kubernetes}} dependency and the custom {{k8smaintainer}} tooling required to manage it, simplifying the build and maintenance process.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* CI - MUST be running successfully with tests automated
* {{PreflightPermissions}} feature gate removed from {{internal/operator-controller/features/features.go}}
* {{internal/operator-controller/authorization/}} package removed entirely (~700 lines: {{PreAuthorizer}}, escalation checker, {{rbacGetter}}, decoded manifest analysis)
* Pre-authorization checks removed from Helm applier ({{helm.go}})
* Pre-authorization checks removed from Boxcutter applier ({{boxcutter.go}})
* {{k8s.io/kubernetes}} dependency removed from {{go.mod}} (both {{require}} and {{replace}} directives)
* {{hack/tools/k8smaintainer/}} tool removed
* {{k8s-pin}} Makefile target removed
* All {{go.mod}} requires lines with {{k8s.io/}} packages agree on the Kubernetes version (e.g. {{v0.36.1}})
* No {{replace}} lines exist in {{go.mod}} for {{k8s.io/}} packages.
* {{verify}} Makefile target simplified (no longer runs {{k8s-pin}})
* RBAC watches on Roles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings cleaned up (if only needed for pre-auth)
* All unit and e2e tests updated

h2. Key code areas

* {{internal/operator-controller/features/features.go}} — remove feature gate
* {{internal/operator-controller/authorization/rbac.go}} + {{rbac_test.go}} — remove entirely

h1. Epic Goal

Remove the {{PreflightPermissions}} alpha feature gate and all associated pre-authorization code, including the {{authorization/}} package and the {{k8s.io/kubernetes}} dependency.

h2. Why is this important?

With OLMv1 adopting cluster-admin scope, pre-authorization checks that validate whether a ServiceAccount has the right permissions before applying manifests are unnecessary — the controller always has permission. Removing this code also eliminates the heavyweight {{k8s.io/kubernetes}} dependency and the custom {{k8smaintainer}} tooling required to manage it, simplifying the build and maintenance process.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* CI - MUST be running successfully with tests automated
* {{PreflightPermissions}} feature gate removed from {{internal/operator-controller/features/features.go}}
* {{internal/operator-controller/authorization/}} package removed entirely (~700 lines: {{PreAuthorizer}}, escalation checker, {{rbacGetter}}, decoded manifest analysis)
* Pre-authorization checks removed from Helm applier ({{helm.go}})
* Pre-authorization checks removed from Boxcutter applier ({{boxcutter.go}})
* {{k8s.io/kubernetes}} dependency removed from {{go.mod}} (both {{require}} and {{replace}} directives)
* {{hack/tools/k8smaintainer/}} tool removed
* {{k8s-pin}} Makefile target removed
* {{verify}} Makefile target simplified (no longer runs {{k8s-pin}})
* RBAC watches on Roles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings cleaned up (if only needed for pre-auth)
* All unit and e2e tests updated

h2. Key code areas

* {{internal/operator-controller/features/features.go}} — remove feature gate
* {{internal/operator-controller/authorization/rbac.go}} + {{rbac_test.go}} — remove entirely
* {{internal/operator-controller/applier/helm.go}} — remove pre-auth check calls
* {{internal/operator-controller/applier/boxcutter.go}} — remove {{runPreAuthorizationChecks}}, {{revisionManagementPerms}}
* {{cmd/operator-controller/main.go}} — remove {{PreflightPermissions}} feature gate check and wiring
* {{go.mod}} — remove {{k8s.io/kubernetes}} require + replace
* {{hack/tools/k8smaintainer/}} — remove entirely
* {{Makefile}} — remove {{k8s-pin}} target, simplify {{verify}}
* {{helm/olmv1/templates/rbac/clusterrole-operator-controller-manager-role.yml}} — remove RBAC watches if only needed for pre-auth

h2. Dependencies

* Blocked by: OPRUN-4629 (Enhancement proposal)

h1. Epic Goal

Make {{ClusterExtension.spec.serviceAccount}} optional, grant operator-controller {{cluster-admin}} RBAC, and always use the operator-controller's own SA for CE and COS reconciliation. This leaves SA-scoped clients and caches in place but always uses the cluster-admin SA.

h2. Why is this important?

This is the core behavioral change that shifts OLMv1 from user-provided SA-scoped operations to controller-owned cluster-admin operations. It eliminates the UX complexity of requiring users to create and configure ServiceAccounts with difficult-to-determine permissions, and aligns the permission model with the architectural reality that OLMv1 is single-tenant.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

* CI - MUST be running successfully with tests automated
* {{ClusterExtension.spec.serviceAccount}} field is optional (no longer required)
* When {{spec.serviceAccount}} is provided, OLMv1 emits a deprecation warning and ignores it
* OLMv1's service account is bound to the {{cluster-admin}} ClusterRole
* OLMv1 always uses its own service account for all interactions with the cluster's apiserver
* Operator-controller's SA is always mapped to CE and COS reconcilers
* Existing ClusterExtensions with {{spec.serviceAccount}} set continue to function (graceful migration)
* CRD upgrade safety is maintained when changing the serviceAccount field from required to optional
* Remove {{ServiceAccountValidator}} reconciliation step
* Remove {{getUserInfo()}} / SA-based {{user.Info}} construction from Helm and Boxcutter appliers
* Remove {{ServiceAccountRestConfigMapper}}, {{TokenGetter}}, {{TokenInjectingRoundTripper}}
* Remove SA annotations on ClusterObjectSet ({{ServiceAccountNameKey}}, {{ServiceAccountNamespaceKey}})
* Emit deprecation warning when {{spec.serviceAccount}} is set

h2. Key code areas

* {{api/v1/clusterextension_types.go}} — make {{spec.serviceAccount}} optional, add deprecation markers
* {{helm/olmv1/templates/rbac/}} — grant {{cluster-admin}} ClusterRole
* {{internal/operator-controller/authentication/tokengetter.go}} — remove
* {{internal/operator-controller/authentication/tripper.go}} — remove
* {{internal/operator-controller/action/restconfig.go}} — remove {{ServiceAccountRestConfigMapper}}
* {{internal/operator-controller/applier/helm.go}} — remove {{getUserInfo()}}, update to use controller's own SA
* {{internal/operator-controller/applier/boxcutter.go}} — remove {{getUserInfo()}}, update to use controller's own SA
* {{internal/operator-controller/controllers/clusterextension_reconcile_steps.go}} — remove {{ServiceAccountValidator}}
* {{internal/operator-controller/controllers/revision_engine_factory.go}} — remove {{createScopedClient}}
* {{internal/operator-controller/labels/labels.go}} — remove SA annotation keys
* {{cmd/operator-controller/main.go}} — rewire to always use controller's own SA

h2. Dependencies

* Blocked by: OPRUN-4675 (Enhancement proposal)

h2. Goal

Design the API for splitting the current ClusterObjectSet into two resources:

* *ClusterObjectSet (COS)* — a mutable resource that clients create and update
* *ClusterObjectSetRevision (COSR)* — an immutable resource stamped out by the COS controller

This follows the Deployment → ReplicaSet pattern from Kubernetes.

h2. Problem

Today, clients creating ClusterObjectSets must first list existing objects to determine the next revision number. This adds complexity, creates race conditions, and couples clients to implementation details of revision ordering.

h2. Proposed Design

h3. ClusterObjectSet (mutable, client-facing)

* Clients create and update a single COS resource
* Spec contains phases, collision protection, progression probes, etc. (mutable)
* May include a {{spec.selector}} to scope its COSRs (like Deployment)
* Perhaps the COS replaces the need for a {{spec.group}} field — the COS itself is the grouping mechanism. Or maybe the COS writes it’s name into COSR.spec.group.
* {{status}} surfaces current revision, rollout conditions, active revisions

h3. ClusterObjectSetRevision (immutable, controller-managed)

* Created by the COS controller when it detects a spec change
* Essentially the current ClusterObjectSet spec: phases, collision protection, lifecycle state — all immutable
* Revision number assigned by the COS controller (single writer, no races)
* {{spec.group}} identifies the parent revision chain, {{spec.revision}} provides numeric ordering
* *Name must equal `{group}-{revision}`* — enforced by CEL validation — giving etcd-level uniqueness for free (no webhook needed)

h3. Key semantic difference from Deployment/ReplicaSet

Unlike ReplicaSets where Pods are fully disjoint, COSRs manage *overlapping objects* that must transfer ownership between revisions. A CRD, Namespace, or Deployment managed by revision N must be handed off to revision N+1 — not deleted and recreated. This means:

* Multiple revisions can be Active simultaneously during handoff
* The COS controller must orchestrate ownership transfer for shared objects
* Revision ordering is load-bearing (determines handoff direction), not just cosmetic
* Old revisions archive only after the new revision has fully rolled out

h3. Standalone usage

COS does not require a parent ClusterExtension. The hierarchy becomes:

{{ClusterExtension (optional) → ClusterObjectSet → ClusterObjectSetRevision}}

h2. Deliverables

* API type definitions for COS and COSR
* CEL validation rules (name == group-revision, immutability constraints)
* Analysis of how COS controller manages revision creation, ownership handoff, archival, and GC

h2. Goal

Design the API for introducing a mutable orchestration layer above the current ClusterObjectSet:

* *ClusterObjectDeployment (COD)* — a mutable resource that clients create and update
* *ClusterObjectSet (COS)* — an immutable revision resource stamped out by the COD controller

This follows the Deployment → ReplicaSet pattern from Kubernetes.

h2. Problem

Today, clients creating ClusterObjectSets must first list existing objects to determine the next revision number. This adds complexity, creates race conditions, and couples clients to implementation details of revision ordering. The ClusterExtension controller also conflates catalog resolution with deployment orchestration (revision stamping, archival, pruning).

h2. Proposed Design

h3. ClusterObjectDeployment (mutable, client-facing)

* Clients create and update a single COD resource
* Spec contains a {{template}} with phases, collision protection, and per-object inline assertions (mutable)
* {{template.metadata}} carries caller-specific labels and annotations (package name, bundle version, etc.) — this is the seam between the resolution and orchestration layers
* {{spec.revisionHistoryLimit}} controls how many archived COSs to retain
* {{status}} surfaces {{Available}} and {{Progressing}} conditions, plus {{activeRevisions}} listing non-archived COSs

h3. ClusterObjectSet (immutable, controller-managed)

* Created by the COD controller when it detects a template change (via SHA-256 hash)
* Contains phases with inline per-object assertions, collision protection, lifecycle state — all immutable except {{lifecycleState}}
* Revision number assigned by the COD controller (single writer, no races)

h2. Background

The team has aligned on a strategy of injecting lifecycle data into all OCP version catalogs for FBC fragments (i.e., fragments that target multiple OCP versions will carry lifecycle data into every catalog they appear in, rather than bifurcating fragments per version). Before proceeding with this approach, we need to validate that the presence of lifecycle data in <5.0 catalogs does not cause on-cluster compatibility or performance issues.

h2. Goal

Determine whether the presence of lifecycle FBC data in <5.0 catalogs causes any of the following:

* *Compatibility issues* — confirm that existing consumers of catalog data (e.g., OLM, console, CLI tooling) on <5.0 clusters gracefully ignore unknown lifecycle fields and do not error or behave unexpectedly.
* *Performance regressions* — catalog size will increase; verify this does not meaningfully impact catalog serving, loading, or resolution times.
* *Customer impact* — verify that production-ready catalogs with lifecycle data do not surface misformatted or confusing information to customers on older clusters.

h2. Testing Matrix

The following version boundaries affect how catalogs are built, served, and consumed. Each combination should be tested with lifecycle data present:

||Dimension||< Boundary||>= Boundary||
|Catalog serving|Pod runs directly (< 4.15)|{{extractContent}} (>= 4.15)|
|CSV metadata format|{{olm.bundle.object}} (< 4.17)|{{olm.csv.metadata}} (>= 4.17)|
|Cache format|JSON (< 4.17)|Pogreb (>= 4.17)|

This gives us the following representative version buckets to test against:

# *< 4.15* — pod-based serving, {{olm.bundle.object}}, JSON cache
# *4.15–4.16* — {{extractContent}} serving, {{olm.bundle.object}}, JSON cache
# *>= 4.17* — {{extractContent}} serving, {{olm.csv.metadata}}, Pogreb cache

Additionally, test modified images using OLMv1 on *4.18* and *4.22* to verify compatibility with the OLMv1 catalog consumption path.

h2. Approach

For each version bucket:

# *Build a modified redhat-operators catalog image* that includes fake (but roughly size-estimated) lifecycle blobs for every package in the catalog.
# *Build the cache* using the same version of opm that IIB uses for that version bucket (upstream builds, iirc).
# *Run `opm validate`* using the same version of opm that IIB uses for that version bucket.
# *Embed the opm binary from the operator-registry OCP payload image* for that version bucket (this is the binary used to serve the catalog at runtime).
# *Run the catalog image on-cluster in the same way as the default catalog* (i.e., matching the serving mechanism for that version bucket) and verify catalog loading, operator resolution, and installation flows work correctly.
# *Document findings* — if lifecycle data causes issues on any bucket, the team will need to reconsider the injection strategy (e.g., bifurcating fragments or stripping lifecycle data for older catalogs).

h2. Context

Hypershift support for the Update Planner (OCPSTRAT-2618) has been confirmed as in-scope by PM (Marina Kalinin, Daniel Messer). This spike is to understand the scope of work required to make the lifecycle-controller/lifecycle-server design work in the Hypershift topology before committing it as release-blocking scope for 5.0 (October timeframe).

The feature is not yet in TPNU on standalone clusters, so adding Hypershift scope carries significant risk.

h2. Current Design Assumptions That Break on Hypershift

# *lifecycle-controller expects a local catalog pod per CatalogSource.* In Hypershift, the default CatalogSources are type {{grpc}} with an address, and Hypershift directly manages the catalog pod lifecycle on the management cluster.
# *Performance optimizations assume co-location.* The lifecycle-server runs on the same node as the catalog pod to avoid pulling large catalog images on multiple nodes, and uses image volume source to directly mount the catalog image. These assumptions might not hold across the management/data-plane split.
# *No use of packagemanifests API or gRPC.* The design deliberately avoids new code in OLMv0, which rules out some existing cross-plane communication paths.
# *Console runs on the data plane, default catalogs run on the management cluster.* This creates a networking gap: the console needs to reach lifecycle metadata, but the data backing it might live on the management cluster side.

h2. Hypershift Topology (as understood)

* Default CatalogSources exist in the managed (guest) cluster’s apiserver in {{openshift-marketplace}}, with the gRPC address directly populated.
* The pods backing those default CatalogSources are directly Hypershift-managed (not CatalogSource-managed) and run in the *management cluster*.
* Custom CatalogSources get normal treatment: their pods run in the *managed cluster*.
* OLMv0’s packageserver and catalog-operator both run in the *management cluster*. They connect as clients to gRPC services in both the management (for default catalogs) and managed (for user catalogs) clusters.
* OLMv0’s packageserver hosts an aggregated API service (packagemanifests) that is registered and accessible via the managed cluster’s apiserver.
* Console runs in the *managed cluster*_._ It uses standard kubernetes APIs against the *managed cluster*’s apiserver (PackageManifests, Subscriptions, CSVs, etc.) to present all cluster information about OLMv0. It does not need to connect to any services running in the management cluster for OLMv0-related UIs.

h2. Potential Approaches Discussed

h3. 1. Hypershift directly manages lifecycle-server pods (skip lifecycle-controller)

Since Hypershift already directly manages catalog pods, it could also manage lifecycle-server pods. Run a static lifecycle-server/service on the management cluster side, then plumb the network from console (managed cluster) to lifecycle-server (management cluster).

* *Pro:* Keeps RH-managed services and data on the management cluster and matches the expectations of co-locating the catalog pods with the lifecycle servers.
* *Cons:*
** Requires punching a hole from the managed cluster into the management cluster to allow Console to access a service in the management cluster.
** Running the lifecycle-controller may not be possible, which may mean custom code and manifests tailored to hypershift.

h3. 2. Run lifecycle-server on the data plane

Push the lifecycle-server into the data-plane compute nodes so console-operator can access it locally with no additional networking.

* *Pro:* No cross-plane networking needed for console.
* *Cons:* 
** Need to get lifecycle data into those pods. ConfigMap may work — raw PLCC data is ~1.5MB and would shrink significantly after trimming to just OLM operators and needed fields. But catalogs are considered cluster infrastructure that shouldn't occupy customer-paid compute.
** This is a significant difference from the current design? Would we change everything to match this design, or would this be specific to Hypershift?

h3. 3. Use Cincinnati/OSUS as lifecycle data proxy (OTA-1964)

Have the Update Service (OSUS) mirror lifecycle data. Data comes via {{oc-mirror}} with {{graph: true}}. Connected clusters can pull directly from the PLCC API.

* *Pro:* Works for disconnected clusters. Avoids catalog-side changes.
* *Con:* Requires customers to install the Cincinnati/Update Service operator. Introduces long-term API compatibility burden with PLCC. Nobody (including lifecycle maintainers) seems clear on the PLCC API stability commitments.  Unclear what firewall/egress rules apply to HyperShift data planes ([+OSDOCS-19450+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-19450]).

h3. 4. Direct PLCC API access from data plane

Have the console or other data-plane consumers pull directly from {{https://access.redhat.com/product-life-cycles/api/v2/products}}.

* *Pro:* Simplest approach for connected clusters.
* *Con:* Doesn't work for disconnected clusters. Introduces long-term API compatibility burden with PLCC.  Unclear what firewall/egress rules apply to HyperShift data planes ([+OSDOCS-19450+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-19450]).

h2. Key Constraints

* Only targeting Red Hat operators (specifically {{redhat-operators}} catalog) for now. Not exposing lifecycle data for non-Red-Hat catalogs.
* Internal API only for 5.0 — no time for proper API review/docs for release-blocking status.
* PLCC API and policies will almost certainly change within 5.0's support lifetime. Any API committed now will need to be maintained for the duration.
* Catalogs are considered cluster infrastructure — contract is that HCP users don't see, control, or pay for enabled catalogs. This may apply to lifecycle-server too.
* October 2026 shipping timeframe is committed for [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2618|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2618|smart-link].

h2. Open Questions

# What are the exact networking/firewall constraints for HyperShift data-plane access to external services or management-cluster services? Who owns the data-plane firewall policy?
# Can the lifecycle-server run on the management cluster side and be accessed from the data plane via existing proxy mechanisms (e.g., Konnectivity)?
# If the lifecycle-server runs on the data plane, does that violate the "catalogs are cluster infrastructure" contract?
# Is the data small enough for ConfigMap transfer from control plane to data plane? (Raw PLCC data is ~1.5MB; trimmed data for just OLM operators should be much smaller.)
# Does the Hypershift team have capacity to add lifecycle-server pod management alongside their existing catalog pod management? Or is this more scope added to the OLM engineering team? Are other resources in the organization available to help?
# Can this be deferred to 5.1 if it's too risky for 5.0? PM has confirmed it's in scope, but the risk/resourcing tradeoff needs explicit acknowledgement.

h2. References

* [OCPSTRAT-2618|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2618] — OpenShift Operator Update Planner - Phase 1
* [OTA-1964|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OTA-1964] — OSUS as product-lifecycle API proxy
* [OSDOCS-19450|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-19450] — HyperShift firewall docs ambiguity
* [OSDOCS-19451|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-19451] — HyperShift firewall docs ambiguity
* [Slack thread|https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/C0AKSDTRK5H/p1777387710168819] — source discussion
* [Lifecycle data schema discussion|https://docs.google.com/document/d/10FmNNzhhiNGC6zEk66-QLyBcJzi3gpMlV_p8tZ5-yUI/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.1oyyxcl2cgvd]

This spike is to understand the scope of work required to make the lifecycle-controller/lifecycle-server design work in the Hypershift topology before committing it as release-blocking scope for 5.0 (October timeframe).

The feature is not yet in TPNU on standalone clusters, so adding Hypershift scope carries significant risk.

h2. Current Design Assumptions That Break on Hypershift

# *lifecycle-controller expects a local catalog pod per CatalogSource.* In Hypershift, the default CatalogSources are type {{grpc}} with an address, and Hypershift directly manages the catalog pod lifecycle on the management cluster.
# *Performance optimizations assume co-location.* The lifecycle-server runs on the same node as the catalog pod to avoid pulling large catalog images on multiple nodes, and uses image volume source to directly mount the catalog image. These assumptions don't hold across the management/data-plane split.
# *No use of packagemanifests API or gRPC.* The design deliberately avoids new code in OLMv0, which rules out some existing cross-plane communication paths.
# *Console runs on the data plane, catalogs run on the management cluster.* This creates a networking gap: the console needs to reach lifecycle metadata, but the data backing it lives on the management cluster side.

h2. Hypershift Topology (as understood)

* Default CatalogSources exist in the managed (guest) cluster in {{openshift-marketplace}}, with addresses pointing to gRPC servers network-accessible from the managed cluster.
* The pods backing those default CatalogSources are directly Hypershift-managed and run in the *management cluster*.
* Custom CatalogSources get normal treatment: their pods run in the *managed cluster*.
* v0 CatalogSources are available via the guest cluster's apiserver (API server continuity is an architectural principle of HCP).
* OLMv1 uses HTTP service endpoints for catalog data (not Kube API), which would require an egress route for cross-plane access.
* Konnectivity sidecars proxy gRPC access, but it's unclear if this fits the use case.

h2. Potential Approaches Discussed

h3. 1. Hypershift directly manages lifecycle-server pods (skip lifecycle-controller)

Since Hypershift already directly manages catalog pods, it could also manage lifecycle-server pods. Run a static lifecycle-server/service on the management cluster side, then plumb the network from console (managed cluster) to lifecycle-server (management cluster).

* *Pro:* Mirrors existing Hypershift catalog management pattern.
* *Con:* Still requires solving management-to-data-plane networking for console access.

h3. 2. Run lifecycle-server on the data plane

Push the lifecycle-server into the data-plane compute nodes so console-operator can access it locally with no additional networking.

* *Pro:* No cross-plane networking needed for console.
* *Con:* Need to get lifecycle data into those pods. ConfigMap may work — raw PLCC data is ~1.5MB and would shrink significantly after trimming to just OLM operators and needed fields. But catalogs are considered cluster infrastructure that shouldn't occupy customer-paid compute.

h3. 3. Use Cincinnati/OSUS as lifecycle data proxy (OTA-1964)

Have the Update Service (OSUS) mirror lifecycle data. Data comes via {{oc-mirror}} with {{graph: true}}. Connected clusters can pull directly from the PLCC API.

* *Pro:* Works for disconnected clusters. Avoids catalog-side changes.
* *Con:* Requires customers to install the Cincinnati/Update Service operator. Introduces long-term API compatibility burden with PLCC. Nobody (including lifecycle maintainers) seems clear on the PLCC API stability commitments.  Unclear what firewall/egress rules apply to HyperShift data planes ([+OSDOCS-19450+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-19450]).

h3. 4. Direct PLCC API access from data plane

Have the console or other data-plane consumers pull directly from {{https://access.redhat.com/product-life-cycles/api/v2/products}}.

* *Pro:* Simplest approach for connected clusters.
* *Con:* Doesn't work for disconnected clusters. Introduces long-term API compatibility burden with PLCC.  Unclear what firewall/egress rules apply to HyperShift data planes ([+OSDOCS-19450+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-19450]).

h2. Key Constraints

* Only targeting Red Hat operators (specifically {{redhat-operators}} catalog) for now. Not exposing lifecycle data for non-Red-Hat catalogs.
* Internal API only for 5.0 — no time for proper API review/docs for release-blocking status.
* PLCC API and policies will almost certainly change within 5.0's support lifetime. Any API committed now will need to be maintained for the duration.
* Catalogs are considered cluster infrastructure — contract is that HCP users don't see, control, or pay for enabled catalogs. This may apply to lifecycle-server too.
* October 2026 shipping timeframe is committed.

h2. Open Questions

# What are the exact networking/firewall constraints for HyperShift data-plane access to external services or management-cluster services? Who owns the data-plane firewall policy?
# Can the lifecycle-server run on the management cluster side and be accessed from the data plane via existing proxy mechanisms (e.g., Konnectivity)?
# If the lifecycle-server runs on the data plane, does that violate the "catalogs are cluster infrastructure" contract?
# Is the data small enough for ConfigMap transfer from control plane to data plane? (Raw PLCC data is ~1.5MB; trimmed data for just OLM operators should be much smaller.)
# Does the Hypershift team have capacity to add lifecycle-server pod management alongside their existing catalog pod management?
# Is PLCC API stability sufficient to commit to a schema for the 5.0 support lifecycle (~5 years with EUS)?
# Can this be deferred to 5.1 if it's too risky for 5.0? PM has confirmed it's in scope, but the risk/resourcing tradeoff needs explicit acknowledgement.

items.toString: Make OTE local output easier to read

*Problem:*
When running OTE locally, it prints one big JSON with all 46 test results.
This is hard to read and makes it difficult to see what failed or changed.

*Note:*
We cannot change this JSON for CI because it’s used by Supy.

*Solution:*
Add a better output for local runs only, for example:

* simple summary of passed/failed tests
* clearer logs per test
* optional flag for readable output

*Acceptance:*

* easier to see failures locally
* CI output stays the same
* no impact on Supy integration
